content.thinking:
I'm sketching the proportions for a whimsical biplane model—roughly real-world scale but chubby and exaggerated—then planning the joint skeleton starting with the fuselage root and working out to the propeller and rudder hinges.

I'm picking a warm toy-like color palette of cream, red, yellow, wood brown, dark trim, metal, rubber, and sky glass, and deciding to build the fuselage with a lofted shape across stations for that rounded, chubby silhouette.

I'm working out the full joint hierarchy under the body root, adding wheels, tail wheel, rudder, elevators, ailerons, and considering a goggled pilot head for extra charm while keeping the rig reasonably simple.

Now I'm defining the fuselage loft stations front-to-back with widths, heights, and vertical offsets to get that bulbous nose tapering into a slim tail, and sketching out a custom cel-shaded paint function that layers a cream base with a red stripe sweep across the flanks.

Writing cowl lathe profile...

I'm positioning the cowl along the lathe axis at the fuselage front station, sizing it slightly larger than the fuselage radius for a chubby look, then working out a paint scheme with a red body and yellow rim band near the opening.

For the engine, I'm placing a dark cylindrical core inside the cowl with seven small radial cylinder pots to suggest an aircraft radial engine, plus a spinner cone at the hub. Then I'm setting up the propeller as two wooden blades extruded from an outline shape attached to the prop joint.

Writing blade outline shapes...

For the two blades, I'm mirroring the second along the opposite y-direction so they extend both up and down, and painting the tips yellow against the wood-colored body for a classic prop look.

Now I'm working out the wing geometry: upper wing sits higher with a wider span, lower wing shorter and positioned near the fuselage bottom, both extruded from a plan-view outline with appropriate chord and thickness.

I'm deciding to keep ailerons simple by adding them as separate thin red scalloped overlay strips on the outer trailing edge of the lower wings, attached via hinge joints rather than cutting them into the main wing outline.

For wing coloring I'm setting most surfaces yellow with red bands along the leading edge and wingtips, plus red along the rim where the surface normal tilts away from vertical, and adding thin dark rib lines spaced across the wing for detail.

For wing thickness, I'll extrude with a slight bevel and keep the upper and lower wing surfaces symmetric, skipping a separate leading-edge tube for simplicity. Next I'm working out the interplane struts, placing two pairs per side connecting from the lower wing upward.

Adding strut rods with wood-grain paint, metal end fittings, diagonal bracing wires between strut tops and bottoms, and cabane struts connecting the fuselage top to the upper wing center.

Now I'm working out how the lower wing passes through the fuselage bottom, then setting up the V-strut landing gear from the fuselage down to wheel axles, with rotated cylinder wheels sized to fit the hinge joints.

Setting tire outer radius to 0.5, placing axle at matching height, and adding a simple cylinder hub along the default y-axis. For the tail wheel, I'm planning a small strut running from the fuselage down to a torus tire, sizing the torus so its bottom touches the ground at y=0.

Now I'm shaping the vertical tail fin in side profile, outlining a rounded-top polygon that tapers from base to tip, with some thickness and a bevel applied along the side-view axes.

I'm then splitting off a separate rudder piece hinged at the rear of the fin, defining its own outline and positioning it slightly further back with a vertical hinge joint so it can pivot.

For the paint scheme I'm giving the fin and rudder red/cream/red horizontal stripes for a cheerful barnstormer look, applied based on vertex position.

Then I'm moving to the stabilizers—laying out a symmetric plan shape centered at the tail, fixed in place, before working out the hinged elevator sections.

Still refining stabilizer-elevator split geometry...

Still working out elevator geometry...

Now I'm setting up stabilizer thickness and paint colors, and planning the cockpit as a dark oval hole in the fuselage top with a coaming ring around it.

Still working out the torus geometry and orientation...

Now I'm sinking a flattened dark disc into the fuselage top to fake a cockpit hole, placing a seat and a pilot figure with a helmet, goggles, and a flowing scarf joined at the body, then starting a thin curved windscreen piece near the cockpit opening.

Building windscreen geometry...

Adding an exhaust pipe stub swept back from the cowl with a flared steel-dark tip, then a cream/red headrest fairing hump as a stretched sphere behind the pilot, and now starting on the tail section of the fuselage.

I'm thinking about adding playful decal details -- a star roundel on the fuselage sides and maybe a number "7" painted inside it, projected onto the curved surface using a decal technique, plus matching roundels on the upper wings for a whimsical touch.

The roundel is symmetric except for the "7" marking, which only goes on the fuselage and needs mirroring depending on which side of the plane it's placed, so I'm working out the orientation based on viewer perspective from each side.

I'll skip the mirror logic since handedness should already be consistent viewed from outside, and drop the scalloped decal idea in favor of simpler painted stripes on the fuselage — defining a red band that sweeps along the length based on a sloping centerline and width function.

Simplifying to a constant centerline with a tapering band width toward the tail, bordered by a thin yellow outline, applied only to the sides and top ridge, while keeping the belly and top deck plain cream.

Now I'm adding a scalloped red band at the front fuselage behind the cowl, edged with a thin yellow trim line, then defining the color palette as a set of named cel-shaded and flat paints (cream, red, yellow, wood, metal, steel, brass, leather, glass, skin, rubber, ink) to stay within the atlas budget, and setting up the rigging with a root body joint and default bone attachment for unassigned parts.

I'm defining small helper functions to create parts and rods bound to specific bones, then laying out the joint hierarchy: the propeller hinge, left and right wheel hinges, and the tail wheel position, each with appropriate parent bones and orientations.

Now I'm placing the tail assembly joints—rudder, elevators, fin, and stabilizer—working out their y-coordinates to match the tapering fuselage stations and making sure the fin and stabilizer overlap correctly at their base.

For the ailerons, I'm figuring out their hinge joints on the upper wing surface and the overlay geometry, aligning the aileron rectangles with the wing's trailing edge z-position.

Checking the trailing edge geometry near the wing tip, I realize the aileron would overhang at the trailing corner if it extends to 3.5, so I'm shrinking it to span x 2.1 to 3.2, a length of 1.1, and working out where the hinge line should sit relative to the trailing edge.

Computing aileron placement and orientation vectors...

Still mapping wing outline coordinates...

Now I'm checking wheel placement against the wing and cowl to avoid collisions -- moving the wheels forward to z=1.35 so the wheel top clears the wing's lower edge, while watching the cowl radius at that same z-range.

I'm working out the gear struts as V-shaped rods connecting the fuselage underside to each wheel, plus an axle rod running between the wheels, and considering whether to add axle fairings before deciding to skip them.

Now I'm positioning the interplane struts between the lower and upper wings at several x-stations, working out z-coordinates for front and rear struts so they align with the tapering wing chords, and noting the wood-grain paint treatment for the struts.

I'm defining the strut cross-section as a streamlined elliptical sweep, working through the orientation logic for how the normal axis aligns with the vertical strut path, then setting up thin wire rods and the diagonal bracing wires between bays, positioning each diagonal to connect opposite corners of the strut bays on both sides of the aircraft.

I'm placing the cabane struts connecting the fuselage top to the upper wing, checking that the attachment points fall within the wing's vertical and depth bounds, then adding small metal fitting boxes at the strut ends and sketching out the radial engine cylinders arranged around a central hub facing forward.

I'm defining the engine pots as small metal cylinders spaced radially, adding a central crankcase cylinder, and lathing a prop spinner dome with a yellow hub ring, then shaping the cowl as a lathed shell opening at the front.

Still writing cowl outline...

Since the cowl radius is larger than the fuselage, there's a front step giving a chubby nose look, so I'll add a red band behind the cowl with a yellow scallop trim line transitioning around z=0.95-1.0.

Now I'm setting up the fuselage loft stations from nose to tail, defining width and height at each z position so the cross-sections taper smoothly into the tail cone, and making sure the lower wing root merges naturally into the fuselage at the right height. I'm using 10-sided circular loft sections for smoothness and keeping the tail cap rounded, with the loft bound to the body bone.

For the cockpit, I'm placing a scaled torus as the coaming ring just above the fuselage top at that station, adding a dark flattened cylinder inside it for the cockpit interior, and positioning a pilot figure with a torso sphere peeking up above the coaming so it reads as a seated pilot.

I'm checking head-to-upper-wing clearance since the pilot's head sphere nearly grazes the wing's trailing edge, so I'm nudging the pilot and cockpit back slightly to avoid overlap while keeping it tucked under the wing. Then I'm sketching the windscreen as an extruded quad shape leaning backward in front of the cockpit opening, positioned low enough to stay clear of the wing above.

Now I'm detailing the pilot figure itself: a leather helmet cap, forward-facing goggle discs with yellow lenses and a strap, a small nose, and a red scarf swept backward using a curved sweep path with tapering radius, all attached under a pilot head joint.

For the arms, I'm giving one a raised waving pose via a capsule from shoulder to hand with a small sphere hand, while the other rests on the cockpit coaming, treating them as rigid parts attached to the body rather than separate joints.

I'm shaping the pilot's head with a helmet hemisphere tilted back, tiny ear flaps, goggles made from brass-rimmed cylinders for the lenses, and a small torus arc for a smiling mouth.

Now I'm positioning the head relative to the torso capsule so it sits naturally at the neck joint, then moving on to wing details like tip navigation lights using small red and green spheres at the wingtips.

Adding stitch lines and a leading-edge color band...

Still writing wing paint logic...

Thinking through ribs and panel lines, then deciding the underside of the wing should always read in shadow tone for a toon look while the top stays lit. I'm sketching a roundel decal as layered circles—red outer ring, cream band, yellow center with a star—plus a teal accent color to give the palette a playful twist.

I'm placing roundel textures on both wings using flat planes positioned just above and below the wing surfaces, aligning them between the struts, and designing a second roundel variant with a bold "7" text overlay for the fuselage. Still need to work out brace wires connecting the tail stabilizer to the fuselage.

I'm defining the hinge joints for the wheels and propeller, then adding finer cowl details -- cooling louvre slits on the sides and a ring of rivets around the cowl rim near the front face.

Rather than placing each rivet as a separate part, I'm merging their sphere geometries into one combined brass mesh using mergeGeometries, translating each sphere into position before merging, and attaching the whole piece to the body bone.

I'm also considering adding a small pennant flag on a pole at the top of the tail fin for a whimsical touch, working out the pole position and a triangular flag outline.

Checking overall proportions: total height about 3.0m with the pennant, wingspan 7.6m, and length roughly 5.3m from prop to tail—comparable to a real Stearman biplane at ~7.3m.

Now I'm working out the ground clearance, making sure the main wheel torus and tail wheel torus geometry sits exactly at floor level (y=0) with no part dipping below it, setting axle heights accordingly so the plane rests in a natural three-point stance.

Setting up the imports and module structure for the aircraft build, making sure every imported utility (mergeGeometries, catmull, paint, svg, INK, zigzag) actually gets used somewhere to avoid typecheck errors, then starting to define the cream color fill and material setup.

Now I'm writing the build function, adding the body and propeller joints with their positions and hinge roles, then working out a helper for creating parts that takes geometry, color, bone joint, and options, pulling in the right types for Joint and PartOptions so everything typechecks cleanly.

Writing wing paint logic...

Confirming n.y direction works with the extrude axes, then moving to the fuselage paint function, which stripes red and yellow bands along a zigzag edge based on position and checks the side normal for additional coloring.

Writing lathe and extrude outlines...

Still building wheel components...

Working out the propeller blade geometry and orientation, making sure the blade planes face the right direction and the tips stay above ground level. I'm setting up wood-grain cel-shaded coloring for the blades and struts using a grain function layered with cel shading.

Now I'm building out the pilot figure: head and helmet geometry, ear flaps, goggles with cylinder lenses, nose, and strap details, positioning each piece relative to the head joint and face plane.

Adding grin, blush, scarf sweep, and torso/arm capsules, checking clearances so the scarf and fuselage don't collide and that colors use the paint/cel conventions consistently.

Shaping the exhaust pipes as swept tubes curving back from the cowl, dark metal, mirrored on both sides.

I need to reroute the exhaust pipe path so it clears the lower wing before it reaches the leading edge, ending the tip around z1.1 with a slightly flared, rounded cap and a dark color.

For the gear, I'm planning simple tube fairings with thin radius, using red-painted struts and wood-toned axles to match the reference coloring.

For the tail wheel, I'm setting up a torus rubber tire with a yellow hub cylinder, attaching it via a hinge joint and connecting a thin metal strut down from the fuselage to the wheel fork.

I'm planning to merge small hardware details—bolts and rivets—into separate batched geometries using boxes and spheres respectively, collecting strut-end positions as I build each strut so I can place wing/strut joint bolts accurately afterward, and I'm also thinking about wingtip light colors like classic red for the left side.

Now I'm positioning wingtip glow lights at the outer rounded tips, working out a pole-mounted pennant with a colored stripe pattern at the tail, and placing the vertical fin outline so its geometry lines up correctly with the fuselage coordinates near the tail section.

I'm then hinging the rudder off the fin's aft edge and sketching the horizontal stabilizer and elevator trapezoid outlines, aligning their leading and trailing edges along the tail's width.

Now I'm working out the bracing wires connecting the fin top and tailplane to the fuselage belly, then writing a reusable strut function that sweeps a rod between two points with a flattened radius profile, plus small boxes marking the fitting points at each end.

I'm placing fittings for upper and lower wing attachment, adding a few cowl louvre boxes positioned along the circular cowl profile, and grouping them by color for merging.

Then I'm scattering small rivet spheres around the cowl rim at regular angular intervals, matching their radius to the cowl's lathed outline at that height, before moving on to positioning the engine cylinders radially around the crankcase center.

Still placing engine details: radial cylinder banks for cylinders, sphere heads, cooling fin rings, a crankcase block, a rear mounting plate, and a propeller shaft extending forward through the cowl opening.

I'm defining the spinner as a lathed shape with a tapered profile, painting it red with a thin yellow accent ring near its base, then positioning the propeller blades just ahead of it so their roots are hidden under the spinner's radius while the blades fan outward.

Now I'm placing a roundel decal on the fuselage side using a sweep target, checking that the position and size sit flush against the surface, then planning matching roundels on the upper and lower wings along with panel lines for hatches and flaps, while deciding to skip extra decorative touches like a sunburst cheek marking or rudder star.

I'm deciding against extra details like seat belts, a hidden instrument panel, a pitot tube rod, or tie-down ropes to keep things simple, and now shifting focus to making sure the code stays TypeScript-strict by only declaring color constants that are actually used, listing out the metal, steel, dark, brass, leather, glass, and skin tone hex values I'll need.

Still defining more colors...

I'm sketching out how to build the plane's textured panels using flat geometry oriented to face different directions—roundel decals on top and underside—plus figuring out the windscreen frame as a set of rods following the glass panel's edges.

Computing the windscreen corner positions and rod placements to connect the base and top of the glass, confirming the windscreen height stays clear of the wing geometry. Now I just need to finalize the rig details like wheels and the propeller hub, then write out the file.
